blocks.text: By the end of the station, you should be able to:
Identify varicose veins and describe their distribution.
Differentiate superficial venous disease from possible deep venous pathology.
Assess for signs of chronic venous insufficiency.
Look for complications such as oedema, skin changes, ulceration and bleeding.
Understand the role and limitations of bedside tests for venous incompetence.
Present your findings and suggest appropriate investigations.
Three venous systems are important.
Runs along the medial foot, leg and thigh, draining into the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction in the groin. Incompetence can produce varicosities along the medial lower limb.
Usually ascends along the posterior calf and drains into the popliteal vein, although its termination varies. Incompetence may produce posterior calf varicosities.

Connect superficial veins to deep veins. Their valves normally direct blood towards the deep system. Incompetence can contribute to venous hypertension and skin damage, particularly around the lower medial leg.
Normally, venous valves and the calf muscle pump promote blood return towards the heart. When valves become incompetent, blood may reflux down the leg, increasing venous pressure when standing.
This can lead to:
Dilated, tortuous superficial veins.
Aching, heaviness and swelling.
Ankle oedema.
Venous eczema and skin pigmentation.
Lipodermatosclerosis.
Venous ulceration.
Deep venous obstruction or previous deep vein thrombosis may also contribute to chronic venous hypertension.
Examination couch.
Adequate lighting.
Measuring tape, if required.
Doppler ultrasound is useful for further assessment but is not routinely required for the initial bedside examination.
A suitable OSCE introduction is:

“Good morning. My name is … I have been asked to examine the veins in your legs. I will inspect both legs while you are standing and lying down, and I may gently feel some of the veins and examine your abdomen and groin if necessary. Is that alright?”
Then:
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the examination and obtain consent.
Ask about pain before palpating.
Ensure privacy and appropriate exposure from the groin to the feet.
Wash your hands.
Arrange a chaperone when appropriate, particularly if examining the groin.
Ask whether the patient can safely stand; provide support if needed.

Important: Varicose veins are best assessed with the patient standing, when gravity distends the superficial veins. If standing is unsafe, examine the patient lying or sitting and document the limitation.

subsections.subsection_title: History you should take before examination

blocks.text: Although the station may focus on examination, examiners commonly ask what history is relevant.
Ask about:
Duration and progression of visible veins.
Aching, heaviness, itching or leg fatigue.
Ankle swelling, particularly towards the end of the day.
Symptoms that worsen with prolonged standing and improve with leg elevation.
Previous bleeding from varicosities.
Previous superficial thrombophlebitis or deep vein thrombosis.
Previous leg ulcers or venous procedures.
Pregnancy history, occupation involving prolonged standing and family history.
Reduced mobility and relevant thrombotic risk factors.
Ask about sudden unilateral swelling, redness or pain because these may suggest DVT rather than uncomplicated varicose veins.
Observe the patient as they stand, if safe.
Look for:
Obvious dilated, tortuous superficial veins.
Asymmetry between the legs.
Swelling of one or both legs.
Skin discolouration.
Dressings or compression stockings.
Previous surgical scars.
Signs of discomfort when standing.
Normal finding: No obvious superficial venous dilatation, asymmetry, oedema or chronic venous skin changes.
Abnormal finding: Prominent, tortuous superficial veins, particularly in the great or small saphenous distribution, suggest varicose veins.

content_groups.group_title: Step 2: Inspect the legs while standing

blocks.text: Inspect the entire lower limb, from the groin to the feet, on both sides.
Identify whether the varicosities occur predominantly:
Along the medial foot, leg and thigh — potentially GSV territory.
Along the posterior calf — potentially SSV territory.
Around the ankle or foot — may accompany advanced venous hypertension.
In irregular clusters — may reflect tributary varicosities or other superficial venous patterns.
Do not assume the precise site of valve incompetence from the visible distribution alone.
Look for the following:

rows: Haemosiderin deposition from chronic venous hypertension
Inflammatory skin changes associated with chronic venous disease
Fibrosis and induration of the lower leg skin and subcutaneous tissue
Small, pale, scar-like areas that may occur in chronic venous disease
Indicates advanced disease or another underlying pathology

blocks.text: A typical venous ulcer is located in the gaiter region, especially near the medial malleolus. It often has an irregular outline, a shallow base and surrounding pigmentation or eczema.
Compare this with an arterial ulcer, which more often affects the toes or pressure points and may have a punched-out appearance with signs of impaired perfusion.
These patterns are suggestive rather than diagnostic.
With the patient standing, gently palpate the affected veins.
Assess:
Whether the veins are soft or firm.
Tenderness.
Localised warmth.
Thrombosed superficial segments.
Oedema and skin induration.
Normal finding: No abnormal superficial venous dilatation, tenderness, induration or oedema.
Abnormal findings:
Soft, compressible, tortuous veins: consistent with uncomplicated varicosities.
A tender, warm, firm cord along a superficial vein: suggests superficial venous thrombosis or thrombophlebitis.
Marked unilateral swelling, pain or warmth: raises concern for DVT and requires prompt assessment.
Do not vigorously massage a painful or swollen leg when DVT is suspected.
Press gently over the shin, ankle or dorsum of the foot for several seconds and observe whether an indentation remains.
Record:
Whether oedema is present.
Whether it is unilateral or bilateral.
Its extent and severity.
Whether it is pitting or non-pitting.
Normal: No peripheral oedema.
Abnormal: Pitting ankle oedema may indicate chronic venous hypertension, but cardiac, renal, hepatic and other causes must also be considered.

content_groups.group_title: Step 5: Assess venous filling and emptying

blocks.text: Observe how the superficial veins behave when the patient changes position.
You may inspect the veins with the patient lying down and then standing, noting how quickly they fill.
Rapid filling may suggest venous reflux or incompetent perforators, but it is not sufficiently reliable to localise the problem or establish a diagnosis on its own.

subsections.subsection_title: Traditional bedside tests for venous incompetence

blocks.text: These tests are frequently discussed in surgical OSCEs. You should understand their principles, but modern clinical practice relies primarily on duplex ultrasound to confirm and map venous reflux.
Purpose: Traditionally used to assess superficial venous valve incompetence and perforator incompetence.
Method:
Lie the patient supine and elevate the leg to empty the superficial veins.
Apply gentle pressure over the saphenofemoral junction in the groin to occlude the superficial venous pathway.
Ask the patient to stand while maintaining the pressure.
Observe the filling of superficial veins.
Release the pressure and observe any additional filling.
Interpretation in the traditional teaching model:
Slow filling while pressure is maintained, followed by rapid filling on release, suggests reflux through the saphenofemoral junction.
Rapid filling despite maintained pressure suggests reflux through incompetent perforators or another pathway.
Limitations: The test has limited accuracy, and interpretation can be difficult in complex venous disease. Do not use it alone to determine which vein requires treatment.
Purpose: Traditionally used to assess deep venous patency in patients with superficial varicosities.
Traditional method:
With the patient standing, apply a tourniquet below the knee to compress superficial veins without obstructing deep venous flow.
Ask the patient to walk or perform repeated heel raises.
Observe changes in superficial vein distension and symptoms.
Traditional interpretation:
Decompression of superficial varicosities may suggest functioning deep venous drainage.
Increasing pain or persistent distension may raise concern about impaired deep venous outflow.

Important limitation: This test is not a reliable method of excluding DVT or deep venous obstruction. If these conditions are suspected, arrange appropriate duplex ultrasound rather than relying on a tourniquet test.

content_groups.group_title: C. Cough impulse at the saphenofemoral junction

blocks.text: Traditionally, the examiner palpates near the saphenofemoral junction in the groin and asks the patient to cough.
A palpable impulse was historically interpreted as evidence of reflux at the junction.
However, this sign is unreliable and should not be used as a definitive test of valve incompetence.

subsections.subsection_title: Examination of the abdomen and groin

blocks.text: This is not always necessary in uncomplicated varicose veins, but it is relevant when the presentation suggests proximal venous obstruction or an atypical pattern.
Inspect and palpate, with consent, for:
Abdominal masses.
Pelvic or abdominal wall collateral veins.
Groin scars from previous venous procedures.
Inguinal masses or lymphadenopathy when clinically relevant.
Prominent atypical veins, especially with sudden onset or marked unilateral swelling, may indicate proximal obstruction and warrant further investigation.
Use this model in the examination.
Normal presentation:

“On examination of both lower limbs, there are no dilated or tortuous superficial veins. There is no lower limb oedema, pigmentation, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis or ulceration. The legs are non-tender, with no palpable superficial thrombosed veins. There are no clinical features of chronic venous insufficiency.
Overall, there is no clinical evidence of varicose veins or their complications.”
Only include findings you have actually assessed. For example, do not claim that deep venous patency has been established solely by normal palpation.

“There are dilated, tortuous superficial veins along the medial aspect of the left leg and thigh, consistent with varicosities in the great saphenous distribution. There is no associated oedema, skin pigmentation, eczema, ulceration or tenderness.
The findings suggest uncomplicated varicose veins. Duplex ultrasound would be appropriate if intervention is being considered.”

“There are dilated superficial veins with pitting ankle oedema, brown pigmentation and eczematous changes in the gaiter region. These findings suggest chronic venous insufficiency with venous hypertension.”

“There is a shallow ulcer near the medial malleolus with an irregular margin and surrounding pigmentation and eczema. The distribution and appearance are suggestive of a venous ulcer. I would assess for arterial disease and infection and arrange appropriate vascular assessment.”

“There is a tender, erythematous, warm, palpable cord along a superficial vein, suggesting superficial venous thrombosis. I would assess the extent of the thrombosis and arrange duplex ultrasound when indicated to exclude associated DVT or extension towards the deep venous system.”

“There is unilateral leg swelling with tenderness and warmth. These findings raise concern for deep vein thrombosis, although they are not diagnostic. I would arrange urgent assessment through the appropriate DVT pathway, including compression duplex ultrasound as indicated.”
Do not delay urgent assessment by completing unnecessary bedside varicose vein tests.
CEAP is a standard classification of chronic venous disease.

rows: No visible or palpable signs of venous disease

blocks.text: The full CEAP classification also includes aetiology, anatomical distribution and pathophysiology.
Exam tip: If a patient has visible varicose veins with oedema, the clinical class is at least C3. If there is an active venous ulcer, the clinical class is C6.
Deep vein thrombosis: Acute unilateral swelling, pain and tenderness.
Superficial venous thrombosis: Tender, warm, palpable cord along a superficial vein.
Lymphoedema: Often involves the foot and toes and may become non-pitting over time.
Chronic heart failure: Often bilateral oedema with other systemic signs.
Peripheral arterial disease: Reduced pulses, cool skin and ischaemic ulceration.
Venous malformations: Atypical vascular lesions that may be present from childhood.

subsections.subsection_title: Management principles an examiner may ask about

blocks.text: Encourage walking, calf muscle exercises and leg elevation when appropriate.
Consider compression therapy only after assessing arterial circulation and contraindications.
Manage venous eczema, skin care and ulcers appropriately.
Refer for duplex ultrasound when intervention is contemplated or when the diagnosis or extent of reflux needs clarification.
Definitive treatment may include endovenous thermal ablation, ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy or surgery, depending on the anatomy, suitability and local services.
Suspected DVT, significant bleeding from varicosities, or a venous ulcer with concerning complications requires prompt assessment.
Examining only one leg.
Forgetting to inspect the patient while standing.
Failing to inspect the medial malleolus for venous ulcers.
Ignoring skin pigmentation and eczema.
Performing Trendelenburg or Perthes tests as if they were definitive modern diagnostic tests.
Assuming that every swollen leg is caused by varicose veins.
Failing to recognise possible DVT or superficial venous thrombosis.
Recommending compression without considering arterial disease.

items: Introduce yourself, obtain consent and expose both legs appropriately
Inspect both legs while standing if safe
Describe the distribution of visible varicosities
Inspect skin pigmentation, eczema, oedema and ulceration
Palpate veins gently for tenderness, warmth and thrombosis
Assess oedema and relevant peripheral pulses
Consider proximal obstruction when the pattern is atypical
Explain traditional venous tests and their limitations
Recognise possible DVT and urgent complications
Present findings and appropriate next steps clearly

blocks.text: Key takeaway: In a varicose vein examination, focus on the distribution of superficial veins, signs of chronic venous hypertension, ulceration and thrombosis. Traditional bedside tests are useful examination knowledge, but duplex ultrasound is the principal investigation for mapping reflux and planning treatment.
